Only five years into its journey, Character.AI, which lets users create AI characters and have conversations with them, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, following a slew of lawsuits and struggles to scale its popular platform. In
a court document
, the company said it had assets and liabilities between $50 million and $100 million.
“Over the past year, Character.ai has taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve its business in the face of significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders,” Character.AI CEO Colin Adams said in a statement.
The startup has also agreed to sell some of its assets to Disney for $20 million, as well as a non-exclusive perpetual license for its technology.
The company said Disney will provide transition services via former Character.AI employees who joined the entertainment giant last month alongside its
former CEO Karandeep Singh Anand
.
Adams said the company would continue operating during the sale process, which is expected to close in late November or early December. However, he did note that there isn’t yet a bid for the company’s assets or a buyer.
“We hope that the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.ai platform. If such a bid is unavailable, however, the platform will be wound down,” Adams wrote.
Character.AI has had a tumultuous five years. Founded by former Google engineers Noam Shazeer, a co-author of the landmark Transformer paper, and Daniel De Freitas in late 2021, the startup initially focused on training foundation models and developing an AI chatbot platform that lets people create custom characters they could chat with.
By September 2022, the startup
reached unicorn valuation with a $150 million fundraise
on the back of high demand for its platform, with the company saying at the time that its users had exchanged more than 2 billion messages with its bots in five months, and active users were averaging more than two hours on the platform daily.
In May 2023, the Character.AI’s apps
attracted
more than 1.7 million installs in their first week after launch. But about a year later, in August 2024, Google struck a $2.7 billion deal to license the startup’s models, and both Shazeer and De Freitas
returned to the search giant
. At that time, the startup’s general counsel, Dominic Perella, stepped in as interim CEO, and the company moved away from training foundation models to focus on growth.
Character.AI’s traction didn’t slow, however, with its platform recording 20 million monthly active users by October of that year.
But things got difficult after the startup was
sued
following the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother says he became obsessed with a chatbot on its platform. Soon after,
Texas launched an investigation
to assess if the platform conformed to child privacy and safety laws. The company subsequently
settled some of these lawsuits
, added more safety features, and banned minors from its platform.
In June of last year, the company appointed Anand, a former Brex and Meta executive, as CEO, and expanded its products to add AI video generation, and social feeds. The company has since tried to introduce new ways to spur user engagement via interactive storytelling formats as well as microdramas.
But the fact that the company had to file for bankruptcy shows that such changes couldn’t move the needle on sustainability for the startup.
It also shows that consumer-facing AI products are really hard to scale and monetize. Character.AI was one of the top apps in terms of time spent, according to analytics firm Sensor Tower. But high engagement can be a double-edged sword; AI costs rise the more people use the app, which consequently also increases the pressure to monetize users.

Character.AI has raised over $193 million in funding across multiple rounds from investors including Lightspeed, SV Angel, Greycroft, and a16z, according to PitchBook.

Emma Roth
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.
An OpenAI engineer was arrested after
the company said it discovered
a “sophisticated recording device” hidden in one of its offices. The employee was identified as Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national. Alfozan is charged with using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications,
according to a press release from the Department of Justice
.
OpenAI’s post about the incident says it used its AI models to “understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier.”
The recording device recovered from a TV in OpenAI’s office.
Image: US Department of Justice
As noted by the DOJ, OpenAI found the device plugged into a TV’s USB port in an executive conference room, where discussions about “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information” often take place.
Alfozan didn’t have access to this room, but CCTV footage allegedly showed him “near the executive conference room on multiple dates prior to the device’s discovery,” according to the DOJ. Footage also captured Alfozan appearing to look behind the TV where the device was installed, federal prosecutors claim.
A photo allegedly showing Alfozan looking behind the TV where the device was installed.
Image: US Department of Justice
The device was covered in toilet paper and installed on or around September 28th. Its contents were encrypted. Additionally, the DOJ claims OpenAI security discovered a bag Alfozan left in another room inside the company’s office, where they found his wallet, ID, and another recording device.
OpenAI says it fired the employee and referred the incident to the FBI. Alfozan was arrested Friday and has remained in custody since, appearing in federal court for the first time on Tuesday.
We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.
At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated.
We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.

Xbox is officially embracing the chaos of AI-powered game ports

Tom Warren
is a senior correspondent and author of
Notepad
, who has been covering all things Microsoft, PC, and tech for over 20 years.
Retro gaming is going through a wild time at the moment, thanks to
decompilations and recompilations
that are letting gamers port classic titles to new devices, or merge code from two different games into a single new experience. Microsoft has witnessed
skateboarding being modded
into
Call of Duty
and
Halo
being
played in a web browser
, and the company is now officially embracing the chaos of this new AI-powered era of game modding.
Microsoft is putting together a new
Xbox Labs group
to explore the rapid emergence of these mods, many of which use AI models to help modders remix games in ways we’ve rarely seen before. Xbox Labs will be a “small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience,”
says Xbox CEO Asha Sharma
. “We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.”
Sharma thinks the experiments we’ve seen in recent weeks, where Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside browsers, “challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games.”
“While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators,” says Sharma. “These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes
because)
they challenge our existing business models.“
Modders are now doing the type of work that Microsoft has been doing for decades with its Xbox backward compatibility program, letting old games run on modern hardware. But they’re doing it without the business model restrictions that Microsoft is tied to. It’s starting to feel like we’re just a model or two away from even more breakthroughs that decouple more modern games from their intended hardware.
Sharma clearly sees an opportunity here, particularly for AI agent use at Xbox. “I think Xbox has an important role to play here,” says Sharma. “Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide.”
Xbox Labs is clearly a way for Microsoft to experiment with how AI will shape where games are played, and Xbox will share any tools and learnings with developers. The bigger question is how Microsoft will respond to decompiles and recompiles of games where modders take its precious IP and make it freely available. Modding is fun, but I can’t see Microsoft and other publishers seeing the fun side if modern console games start to appear where they shouldn’t.
I asked Microsoft to comment about unauthorized IP use, but the company didn’t respond in time for publication.
Here’s Sharma’s full memo:
Team,
The first video games emerged some 75 years ago. In the time since, there have been booms and busts, but every year there are more great games to play, more devices to play them, and best of all, more people than ever playing. That growth helped make XBOX what it is today, and we’ve helped shape the industry in return, from bringing hard drives to consoles and online gaming through Xbox Live to Game Pass and cloud gaming, alongside franchises that have brought millions of people together.
In recent weeks, we’ve seen games rapidly decompiled and rebuilt to run on hardware they were never originally designed to support. Windows PC builds have been translated to run on Apple Silicon or ported to run inside a browser through WebAssembly and WebGPU, the latter now approaching 90% global browser support. Perhaps more surprisingly, we’ve seen many of the biggest games in the world have been remixed into the source code of another.
These experiments challenge long-held assumptions about our industry: the tether between software and hardware, the boundary between creation and play, and how people discover and experience games. While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators. These are unmistakably good outcomes for players, even when (and sometimes
because)
they challenge our existing business models. To explore these possibilities, I’ve asked Scott to stand-up XBOX LABS, a small group of game makers, engineers and scientists whose job is to turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience. We’ll build in the open, learn from what people do, and measure success by whether more people are playing and creating.
I think XBOX has an important role to play here. Coding became the first major workload for agents because they can write, run, and test software. Games share many of those same properties, and people spend more than 72 billion hours a year playing XBOX games, roughly five times the estimated time spent writing code worldwide. We’ve spent 25 years learning how to make great games, and I want our game makers to help shape what these new technologies make possible. As we learn, we’ll share the tools we build with developers across the industry, just as we always have.
Our priorities aren’t changing. We remain committed to the 4Cs, to making great games, to our hardware and to being responsible stewards of IP and the communities built around it. LABS gives us a way to explore new technology without abandoning the work already underway.
Asha

I don’t miss the camera on the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses
It’s harder to be a perv in these audio-only glasses, but removing the ick does make them less ‘useful.’
by

Victoria Song
is a senior reporter and author of the
Optimizer
newsletter. She has more than 13 years of experience reporting on wearables, health tech, and more. Before coming to The Verge, she worked for Gizmodo and PC Magazine.
The other day I whizzed past several people while running in the park, my playlist blasting at full volume. The next morning, I smiled at a barista while ordering a caramel apple-flavored matcha latte. Afterward, I sat on a park bench reading a book, called up a pal to chat about her recent trip to Prague, and then asked my Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses what meetings were coming up on my calendar. The chipper AI voice said I hadn’t connected my Google Calendar yet (I had) and asked if I would like help connecting. I sighed and then asked it to play an upbeat song. It picked Kendrick Lamar’s “Not Like Us.”
These past few days, dozens of people have seen or interacted with me while wearing smart glasses. Not a single person noticed. Probably because these audio-only versions look just like normal glasses. They come in a retro Clubmaster look — like the ones pictured in this review — or a more Wayfarer-esque Burbank style. Honestly, people usually don’t notice when I wear camera glasses either. But for once, I didn’t feel like a creep.

How we rate and review products
The audio-only Ray-Bans aren’t a novel concept. Seven years ago, I strutted around Manhattan taking calls and listening to tunes in the
Bose Frames
, which
also
combined Bluetooth audio with stylish sunglasses. Nobody noticed me in the Bose back then, either. What makes
this
pair notable is that it’s 2026, they’re made by Meta, and, well, there’s been vigorous discourse about whether smart glasses are a form of spyware.
Let’s get privacy out of the way. During setup, all the privacy and data opt-out disclosures were much more prominent than when I’ve previously tested Meta glasses. A screen explained how visual data from AI experiences is handled. (You can opt out of Meta using that data to improve AI; voice data, however, is still used.) There’s no visual data from these glasses — this is simply the new messaging for
any
pair of Meta glasses. You can also opt out of sharing “additional data” with Meta as well, which is
enumerated in a separate document online
. This is a good thing, though it doesn’t address what makes people uncomfortable about smart glasses: the uneasy feeling that someone else is recording you.
You know what sort of
does
, though? Removing the camera. The Bose Frames never triggered the same level of distrust because they were “just” sunglasses-shaped headphones. That applies here too. Frankly, I felt much lighter wearing these out into the world precisely because I couldn’t record footage of anyone. (Even if I feel lame saying “Hey Meta” in public.)
You can see the small, customizable action button on the right-hand temple arm. I programmed it to bring up Meta AI so I don’t have to say “Hey Meta” in public.
I can imagine people still distrusting these Ray-Bans because they have always-listening capabilities for waking up the AI assistant. However, you can disable the wake word in settings and use a customizable button on the right temple arm instead. (This automatically feels 10 percent less silly if you “must” talk to AI assistants outside the home.) There’s no native way to record a conversation directly from the glasses. Any other audio-based feature, like live translation, has to be manually started.
I’m not saying these
can’t
be modded or used for evil out of the box. Where there’s a perverse mind and ill will, there’s a way. I’m saying it’d take more effort because these glasses simply don’t
do
very much.
At least, not yet.
Meta’s Muse AI is eventually coming to the glasses, but it’s not available right now. Right now, the glasses ship with the less powerful Muse Spark model. It’s better than what was on the Ray-Bans in 2023, but it’s still
meh
unless
you’re using it for accessibility reasons
. In which case, these glasses may not be the best use of $350. A camera-equipped model is more helpful for low-vision and blind users. For hard-of-hearing users, the FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature isn’t available yet, and for deaf users, the
Meta Ray-Ban Display
may be more useful because they support live captioning.
Without a camera, the temple arms are much thinner, too.
For everyone else, Muse Spark is nerfed without the camera but can still come in handy. For example, granting access to your messaging apps, Google Calendar, and email lets it do some light scheduling and correspondence on your behalf. If you enable location sharing, you can send where you are to the group chat. It’s
fine
for these tasks, but not great. It’s adept at short queries like “What’s my next calendar event?” or “Set a reminder to update my editors at 12PM.” With more complex asks, I’ve found Muse Spark gets confused, and it’s faster to whip out my phone. I ended up mostly asking it to set reminders for to-dos I remembered while in the middle of something else.
Muse Spark can also give you local recommendations and turn-by-turn audio directions while walking. As I’ve
written before
, that’s great if you’re traveling. Less so if you’re familiar with your local haunts. In my neighborhood, I already know which coffee shops have the best Wi-Fi and snacks — and it wasn’t the one Muse Spark suggested. As for walking directions, they’re not something I need
that
often. When I did, I found using Google Maps on my phone more helpful for getting my bearings.
I’m sure Muse will open up more possibilities when it arrives later this year. Then again,
I’ve seen demos
, and I’m still skeptical that agentic AI will be
the
thing that convinces people to buy smart glasses.
So what
do
I like about these? They’re simply a good pair of open-ear headphones.
I said good, not great. Sound quality is decent, but you’re still dealing with all the tradeoffs that come with this form factor. They struggle at louder volumes. The trebles start to get tinny, and bass can sound distorted. There’s inevitably sound leakage. My spouse frequently reminded me that they could hear everything I was listening to, all of the AI’s responses, and my phone calls. Conversely, even at top volume, ambient noise can still drown out your content. These won’t cut it on a loud subway, for instance.
Still, it’s nice to listen to audiobooks around the house without jumping out of my skin anytime my spouse or cats want my attention. On my daily walks, I’m less afraid of my maniac neighbors mowing me down in their murder mobiles. (New Jersey drivers, man.) It’s not mind-blowing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to my day-to-day routine. And I don’t have to think too hard about it.
You can’t really tell that these are smart glasses unless you look really closely at the transparent portion of the arms.
At 43 to 47g, these are also much comfier than
every
other
pair
of
Meta
glasses
I’ve tried. So far, I’ve worn them for two full days, including a 30-minute run and multiple walks, with zero issues. My Clubmaster review unit also has nose pads — huzzah for anyone with a low nose bridge. That also made for a huge improvement in call quality since the mic for calls wasn’t smushed up against my schnoz. The temple tips can also be adjusted for a better fit.
I usually ding smart glasses for not supporting my -10 prescription and severe astigmatism. These support a range of -12 to +6 — I’m still waiting on a prescription pair, but at least my garbage eyeballs don’t preclude me from wearing these as my daily glasses. All in all, these glasses will fit a much broader range of faces and vision needs.
Battery life is also phenomenal. I was able to eke out two full workdays
without
sticking the glasses back into the case.
Okay, I lied — one more gripe. These feel expensive for headphone glasses that don’t do much yet. The Meta Glasses, for example, now start at $250 and technically do more. These are $100 more for what, exactly? The Ray-Ban branding? The privilege of
not
worrying about freaking out other people? If these were $150 or $200, I’d say these would be a no-brainer. Starting at $350 without prescription lenses, without the hearing assistance features, without Muse? That feels off.
But pricing complaints aside, I didn’t miss the camera. (I only ever use it to take cat videos anyway.) Muse Spark isn’t what I’d call the most compelling AI model, but it’s useful now and then. For the casual user, the headphones are the most useful part of smart glasses.
This is me wondering how my beat went from tracking steps to discussing wearable surveillance and hoping bystanders won’t punch me.
I wish I could just thrust these into the air and declare that nixing the camera solves the privacy problem. I can’t. Yes, I’m relieved that I don’t have to worry about people punching me in the face if I wear these out and about. I
don’t
think most people want more than this right now. Still, I’d be lying if I said I didn’t personally know several people who
would
miss the camera. Not because they’re perverts, but because they find them to be genuinely useful tools for candid home videos, content creation, accessibility, or multimodal AI. For those people, this type of smart glasses isn’t a real option.
Besides, who’s to say Meta won’t add more ambient listening features down the line? Then what? The lack of a camera is only a comfort
for now
. It doesn’t negate the need for continued, thoughtful discussion about AI wearables,
the definition of recording
, and what role these gadgets ought to play in our

articles.content:
Title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control

Published Time: 2026-10-13T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.

Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026.

In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place _and_ how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.

## Growing our monorepo

Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.

Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.

As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a _compressed_ working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.

The typical setup for scaling git checkouts.

Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like?

## Principles for agent-scale source control

With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s [Piper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piper_(source_control_system)) and Meta’s [Sapling](https://sapling-scm.com/), so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are:

**Clients are always online.** Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it.

**Client-server asymmetry.** In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally.

**A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications.**With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control.

**Everything must be horizontally scalable.**At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed.

**Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free.** In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because _global_ state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem.

**The working copy is optional, and sparse by design.** Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads.

## How Scion works

It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle.

### Data structures

In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent,[1](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/redesigning-source-control#footnote-1) along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly.

The shape of a changeset in Scion.

This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets.

A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents.

This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search.

### Scaling Scion

A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner.

Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own.

Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Title: Embedding Gemma Transcribe

URL Source: https://eg2.haku.sh/

Markdown Content:
Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model. We turned it into a speech-to-text model: _an hour of audio in about 13 seconds on a base MacBook Air_, entirely on device.

[Download for Mac (free)](https://eg2.haku.sh/download)v1.6 · macOS 14+ · Apple Silicon
models download on first launch (715 MB)

## Can an embedding model transcribe speech?

EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model: text, images, audio and video in one shared space. Say a word out loud and its audio lands close to the written word.

So we tried reading words straight out of that space.

## How it works

1.   EmbeddingGemma 2's audio encoder stays exactly as it is.
2.   A small reader moves each short slice of audio into the model's text space.
3.   The closest of ~229,000 English words wins, and the slices become a transcript.
4.   A tiny extra model adds punctuation and capitals.

Only the reader is trained: under two hours on 8×H100, on openly licensed English speech. The base model was never trained for speech-to-text.

## How fast?

| Model | Runs on | Mac | Speed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Embedding Gemma Transcribe | Neural Engine | base M3 MacBook Air, 8 GB | 288×1 hour in 12.6 s |
| IBM Granite Speech 5.0 TurboCTC | GPU (MLX) | base M3 MacBook Air, 8 GB | ~150×1 hour in 25.7 s |
| NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (FluidAudio) | Neural Engine | M4 Pro | 156× |
| NVIDIA Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 (FluidAudio) | Neural Engine | M5 Pro | 335× |
| Phonon-2, a Parakeet v3 fine-tune (FluidAudio) | Neural Engine | M5 Pro | 480× |

× real time: seconds of audio per second of processing. Rows 1–2: our tests on the same base M3 MacBook Air. Rows 3–5: [FluidAudio's published benchmarks](https://github.com/FluidInference/FluidAudio/blob/main/Documentation/Benchmarks.md) on larger, newer Macs and different audio. A rough guide, not a like-for-like ranking.

## Where it stands

Its word error rate is about 5% right now, against 2–3% for leading speech models. We believe a better-trained reader can close that gap; that's the next iteration.

## Use it

Drop in an audio file, or hold Right Option, speak and release to dictate into any app. It runs on the Mac's Neural Engine; your audio never leaves the machine.

Title: Sammy's Blog

URL Source: https://www.sammystraus.com/

Markdown Content:
## Table of Contents

*   [1. I posted to HN, and then my website was flooded with AI BOT traffic](https://www.sammystraus.com/#i-posted-to-hn-and-then-my-website-was-flooded-with-ai-bot-traffic)
*   [2. Using LLMs to Make the Emacs Web Browser Great Again](https://www.sammystraus.com/#using-llms-to-make-the-emacs-web-browser-great-again)
*   [3. If technology got better, why did everything get worse?](https://www.sammystraus.com/#if-technology-got-better-why-did-everything-get-worse)
*   [6. Building Chess in about 350 lines of Clojure](https://www.sammystraus.com/#building-chess-in-about-350-lines-of-clojure)
*   [7. Announcing Deft: A class and interface system for Clojure and ClojureScript](https://www.sammystraus.com/#announcing-deft-a-class-and-interface-system-for-clojure-and-clojurescript)
*   [10. The Power Of Habit (Book Review Pt 1)](https://www.sammystraus.com/#the-power-of-habit-book-review-pt-1)
*   [15. The Wonky Math behind the Democratic Primary](https://www.sammystraus.com/#the-wonky-math-behind-the-democratic-primary)

## 1. I posted to HN, and then my website was flooded with AI BOT traffic

For the past few years, I've been working on [sprinklz.io](https://sprinklz.io/), a customizable feed reader that can, among other things, deprioritize certain topics from your news feed.

A month ago, I [posted it to HN](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49660482), and it got a hundred or so upvotes, nice! It seems like people are really tired of hearing about LLMs, and they enjoyed being able to deprioritize them from their feed. It was a good demo of why a tool like this is useful. Everything was looking up, and then…

My website got slow. Like, really, painfully slow. At first I chalked it up to the extra attention of a suddenly popular post. Like any developer I both celebrated, and vowed to make my website more resiliant in the future. Strangely though, the slowness continued, and even started to get worse _several days after_ my post went live, and the metrics I did log did not make sense. Like, you know, a good handful of genuinely active, logged-in users, and a sever exhibiting exhorbatantly high load.

So I took a look at some data. I added top-level logging for every endpoint (how many times was a request made to each url path), and I found that a majority of the requests did not even make an attempt to fetch news articles! For reference, my website is built as a single-page-application, and what this means is that a majority of the requests did not even run the javascript necessary to render the page (!).

Digging further, I looked at aggregate NGINX logs to find abusers, and, you're never going to believe this, but it turns out that nearly half of our traffic was coming from one _specific_ user. I won't name names, but I looked them up, and they describe themselves as a service that listens for changes to a website, and then summarizes them into an AI slop news letter. And by 'listens to changes' I mean query our website many many times per-minute. Blocked.

Several of the others were your standard known crawlers, and kindly identified themselves as such. Claude bot, OpenAI bot, google's search indexer, and several others. I even picked up a few vulnerability scanners along the way. At least, somebody is trying to access -/wp-content/phpinfo.php (my website is not a wordpress site). I added robots.txt to discourage most of the AI scanners, but allow google-bot and other search-related traffic, and asked claude to query all the vulnerability paths and mimic the scanners to make sure I wasn't leaking anything. I also added reasonable rate limits, etc., etc.

The most important lesson though, is that it's time to make my website faster. I want to be the website that _can_ day handle xxx QPS of real traffic, and it should scale better than it did, even under heavy load. Inspired by this encounter, I've made quite a few improvements to the underlying infrastructure over the past few weeks, and these should result in pretty substantial performance gains for all users.

P.S. if you'd like to check it out, the website is fully free, and available [here](https://sprinklz.io/)

The TLDR is that it lets you define your own customizations, _in addition_ to things like the points totals from hacker news. You can use it to filter out topics, like AI or LLMs, but the topics are completely arbitrary and you can program your own customizations.

## 2. Using LLMs to Make the Emacs Web Browser Great Again

When I tell people about the emacs web browser, their first reaction is 'Wait emacs has a web browser?!', followed by, 'yeah… I guess that's kind of a web browser'.

The emacs web browser is designed to render webpages in a terminal-based, textonly environment and, well, it goes about exactly the way you'd expect. It works well on HTML-only, small-content websites, but not so good for anything else.

The problem is that emacs is primarily a text-only editor, but the modern internet is very much _not_ plain-text based. _Simple_ HTML, designed in the _simple_ style of the 1990s has a clear translation into plain text, but _modern_ UI design, with it's visual styling, heavy javascript, and just, overall chaos, not so much.

The emacs web browser would be great, if only we could find a way to go back in time…

Ok, so the plan is simple. We take modern webpages, rewrite their source code into old-school simply-styled HTML, and then pipe it through to the emacs web browser. We just need to find a way to do this easily and at scale.

So um, you didn't forget about LLMs did you? It's nice to be using them in a way that will hopefully _reduce_ the amount of spam content in the world.

Basically, the plan is we write a program that:

*   Opens a webpage in firefox
*   Loads the page and runs all the javascript
*   Asks an LLM to generate a **re-usable program** that transforms the current-page's contents into simplified text
*   Inject the generated javascript into the firefox browser
*   Grab the new page source and forward it to emacs web browser.

Yeah, and so, I've been using it, and it runs very well. Like realistically I can use this on many webpages where eww (emacs web wowser) did not run previously.

Below are some examples of before and after:

The docs for Clojure's mapcat

Figure 1: (before) Using eww-readable

Figure 2: (after) Using simpleweb-simplify-page

It takes a moment to generate the initial modifier program, but once it's generated, it runs pretty fast, and during day-to-day browsing, it mostly doesn't need any extra LLM calls. I have been using it myself and enjoying the experience.

The source code lives here: [https://github.com/sstraust/simpleweb](https://github.com/sstraust/simpleweb)

and is open-source, and free to install, etc., etc.

## 2. If technology got better, why did everything get worse?

I think we all know the answer to this: bad incentives.

Technology makes systems more productive, but it does not, in fact, make _you_ in particular more productive. The tools that enable computers to be more efficient also enable _people_ to be more efficient at exploiting your time, attention, and wellbeing. I'm talking neural nets babyyy.

I first noticed the problem in 2018. Or rather, I noticed that _I_ had a problem, and that problem was spendinng 3 hours a day watching starcraft 2 replays and wondering where the time went, and how I managed to stay up til 2am again.

What's interesting to me is that I didn't have any of these problems until the late 2010s. I had a computer with an internet connection since at least the mid 2000s, and a smartphone with twitter and reddit and the like not long after. It's possible that I've gotten less resiliant over the years, but I have a sneaking suspiscion that it's the computers who changed.

I can't quite put my finger on it, but I have this sensation that every time I interact with a system or website, I'm playing this kind of adversarial game, where I'm trying to just go about my day, and maybe read a little article about computers, and they're trying to figure out a way to keep me on their site for just a little bit longer.

I also have this feeling that as software engineering has moved from a discipline of hobbyists and enthusiasts to leaders who increasingly developed through finance or business-minded tracks, we've found ourselves with these major tools that we used to love become both extremely bland and extremely profitable.

So what can we do it make it stop?

1.   touch grass. really when the world is like this, i think the best solution is to just leave. it's not easy, especially when the planning is often online, but if you can set it up, I promise that a day in the park playing chess with your friends is better than any amount of time you can spend on the internet.
2.   take to the streets. i think that protesting is effective, and more people should do it. if you're willing to take action, it models to others that they can take action.
3.   stop coming back to the same machines. I think we all have this gamblers fallacy in us, where if it didn't pay out the first time, but it pays out sometimes, we try the machine again, but it doesn't really work like that. if you're losing money the lesson is to stop putting coins in the machine.

editor's note: I've been working on a free [customizable news reader](https://sprinklz.io/) as a way to take out some of my frustrations with the modern internet. if you don't use this one, I recommend following individual blogs and websites, because it's so much better to just get off these big platforms entirely.

editors note 2: i haven't yet posted this latest article to my rss xml, because i'm not ready to send notifications for it yet. will add in the coming weeks.

## 3. Deft version 0.2.0

Now that [deft 0.2.0](https://github.com/sstraust/deft) is released, I figure it's a good time to talk about what I built, and why I built it.

The _point_ of Clojure's everything-is-a-map toolkit is that getters and setters are a waste of time. Clojure was built, in large part, in response to the crappy 2008 Java workflow, where you had to write getters, setters, and builders, and you took on all this bloat that nobody enjoyed.

The _problem_ is that if you want to represent your data using the built-in defprotocol and defrecord, and you want to define functions that depend on the presence of a certain field, then the only way to _encode_ that information into the protocol is to add getter and setter metohds to it. icky.

You can also use a combination of protocol + malli schema to represent this, but then when you use it, you need to specify 'this function takes as input something that both implements this protocol _and_ implements this Malli schema'. Also icky.

What we _want_ is something we can use in the style of defprotocol and defrecord, but gives us all the getters and setters and map-like stuff by default. The key insight is that if a field exists in a record, we get all the other good stuff, so we just need to add support for protocols with required keys.

Deft v0.2.0 adds support for namespaced keys in type and protocol definitions. i.e., you can now do:

(defp Positioned :required-keys [::pos - ::Point])

and

(deft Circle [::location/position radius])

(>Circle ::location/position [1 2] :radius 12)

this is useful because you can now define methods that _depend on those fields being present_ i.e.:

(defp Gremlin :extends [location/Positioned])

(defmethod game-object/get-hitbox ::Gremlin [self]
  (js/Matter.Bodies.rectangle
   (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/x])
   (get-in self [::location/pos ::location/y])
   15 15))

Check it out!

articles.content:
Title: Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics

URL Source: https://developers.googleblog.com/gemini-4-argon-for-robotics/

Published Time: 2026-10-13

Markdown Content:
OCT. 13, 2026

Gemini 4 Argon marks a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning—unlocking new workflows across the robotics stack and accelerating progress toward physical AGI.

You can see this leap in capability on the [Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark](https://github.com/embodiedreasoning/ERQA), which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments. Using pure reasoning, Argon scores 87%, outperforming every other frontier model.

As a general-purpose physical reasoning model, Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle. In this post, we share representative prompts for Argon across four key areas:

*   **Robot control →** Mobile manipulation with [MuJoCo](https://mujoco.org/) practice, zero-shot robot control, and closed-loop steering of video world models.
*   **Real2Sim →** Reconstructing physically calibrated simulation twins from robot camera feeds, egocentric human video, or hand-drawn paper sketches.
*   **Physical understanding →** Agentic multimodal hindsight labeling including detailed understanding of dexterity, dense value functions and progress estimation.
*   **Research and self-improvement →** Action improvement via simulation and iterative self-improvement on hardware.

## **Unlocking robot control with Argon**

### **1. Spot mobile manipulation: Putting in the trash bin with MuJoCo practice**

Argon controls a Boston Dynamics Spot® quadruped (12-DoF legs + 6-DoF arm) to learn a new skill: stepping on a foot-pedal trash bin to throw away soda cans. Argon creates an articulated MuJoCo digital twin of a foot-pedal trash bin to practice its moves before stepping on the physical pedal and dropping soda cans into the open bin.

Spot Mobile Manipulation — Real-to-Sim-to-Real foot-pedal trash bin disposal: Spot picking up the soda can, checking its wrist camera, practicing 3-leg tripod balance in MuJoCo, stepping on the foot pedal, verifying hand centering in the open bin, and dropping the can inside.

_Prompt:_

```
There's a Diet Coke can behind you and another on the black table on your left.
Use the spot-mobile-manipulation skill to pick them up and trash them in the black foot-pedal bin.
Before stepping down on the pedal, verify in the front cameras that your front-right foot target is centered on the pedal, and use a 2-agent verification swarm (foot-verifier and hand-verifier) to verify both the foot-pedal step and the 3D hand-in-bin alignment before releasing.
```

Plain text

Copied

### **2. Zero-shot control**

Argon controls a simple robotic arm to place a fallen mug upright and put the crumpled napkin inside. Argon reasons with a visual coordinate harness and action primitives to perform this task over several turns.

Left: 3rd-person real robot view; Right: calibrated wrist camera with projected 2 cm world coordinates and jaw-closing reticle.

_Prompt:_

```
[Attached: wrist_cam.png, obs.json]

Task: Get the robot arm to reorient the mug upright and put the napkin inside the mug.

## Execution Discipline
- Simply output 1 sentence observation followed immediately by your `curl` command (with `# Plan:` on Turn 1 and `# Thought:` on every turn). Everything needed is in `obs.json` and the calibrated reticle/grid drawn on `wrist_cam.png`.

## Visual Coordinate Reference (Annotated on wrist_cam.png)
- `+X` (UP in image): Away from robot base | `-X` (DOWN): Towards robot base
- `+Y` (LEFT in image): World left         | `-Y` (RIGHT): World right
- `+Z`: Height above table                | `Yellow numbers`: World (X, Y) in centimetres (2 cm grid at `grid_z`)
- `Cyan + crosshair`: Current 3D pinch center
- `Cyan [ + ] brackets`: Current jaw opening and closing line
- `Green line`: Current object long-axis orientation (`yaw_deg`: 0° = vertical along +X, 90° = horizontal along +Y)
- `pitch_deg = 90°`: Straight down (-Z) top-down grasp/place; `pitch_deg < 60°`: Tilted coaxial approach along finger axis

## Closed-Loop Turn Workflow
1. Inspect current state & view `wrist_cam.png`:
   `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8081/obs` (returns `ee_pos`, `holding`, `status`, `workspace`, `wrist_cam_path`).
2. Select VLM call granularity upfront on Turn 1:
   - Coarse (2–4 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> `place` -> `done`
   - Pre-Grasp Hover Verify (4–7 calls): `look_at` -> `goto(z=0.04)` (verify cyan `[ + ]` brackets straddle target) -> `grasp` -> `place_until_contact` -> `done`
   - Fine Visual Servoing (8–20 calls): `look_at` -> `grasp` -> pre-pose `goto` -> closed-loop `move_by` / `move_until_contact` -> `done`
3. Send motion primitives (`POST /plan`) and verify visually after every turn in the updated `wrist_cam.png`. If `status == "grasp_failed"`, call `robot.look_at(...)` to re-observe and recover closed-loop.

## Code-as-Policies Primitives (`POST http://127.0.0.1:8081/plan`)
robot.look_at(x=0.35, y=0.13, z=0.14, grid_z=0.015)
x, y = robot.deproject(u=0.52, v=0.48, z_plane=0.015)
robot.grasp(x=x, y=y, z=0.015, yaw_deg=-35, pitch_deg=90)
robot.place(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.075)
robot.place_until_contact(x=0.24, y=0.06, z=0.015, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002)
robot.goto(x=0.28, y=0.05, z=0.04, arc_z=0.14, pitch_deg=25, azimuth_deg=90, roll_deg=0, speed=0.10)
robot.move_by(forward=0.025, dz=-0.002, dpitch_deg=-3, droll_deg=5, speed=0.04)
robot.move_until_contact(dz=-0.06, speed=0.03, max_lag=0.012, relief=0.002)
robot.open_gripper() / robot.close_gripper() / robot.home() / robot.done()
```

Plain text

Copied

### **3. Omni control**

Argon steers robots in the Gemini Omni World Model to rearrange five scattered Scrabble tiles (`G, R, A, N, O`) into a clean row spelling `A - R - G - O - N`. Instead of specifying one static prompt, Argon steers in a closed visual loop. It writes timestamped action prompts, inspecting intermediate rollout keyframes, and refining its prompts.

Iterative Video World Model Steering Dexterous Hands: 33-Step Steered Video Rollout Spelling A-R-G-O-N.

_Prompt:_

```
Goal: {task_goal}

You are steering a video world model (Gemini Omni) in an iterative visual feedback loop. Inspect the attached frames from the latest rollout and write the next timestamped action prompt for the video world model:
- Break complex motions into one simple, single-direction action at a time.
- Keep inactive hands retracted and avoid blocking the camera's view of objects in the workspace.
- Explicitly state which areas of the workspace become empty after an object moves.
- Use [MM:SS.mmm] timestamps for each action beat and wrap your output in <omni_prompt> tags.

Example format (sample timestamps only, not the full prompt):
<omni_prompt>
[00:00.000] Character A's left hand rests at the side while the right hand reaches toward the target object.
[00:02.500] Character A's right fingertips push the object smoothly into the center of the table, leaving its starting area empty.
[00:05.000] Character A's right hand opens and retracts to the side so all placed objects remain in clear view of the camera.
</omni_prompt>
```

Plain text

Copied

## **Unlocking Real2Sim with Argon**

### **1. Robot view to simulation**

Argon views a real robot teleoperation episode and develops a digital twin; it obtains or creates simulation assets that look and behave like the real objects upon contact with the dexterous hands. Argon tunes the assets and scenes to match sim visuals and contact events with those in the real recorded data in an iterative visual-reasoning loop.

Left (Real View): synchronized real robot camera feeds; Right (Simulated): 3D MuJoCo scene reconstructed and calibrated by Argon.

_Prompt:_

```
[Attached: robot_rollout_episode]

Build a MuJoCo scene of the robot and reconstructed task objects. When each episode is replayed frame by frame, by driving the robot joints toward the logged observation.state with joint-space PD.

Iterate using two verification objectives:
(1) Visual match: MuJoCo renders from the head_left, left_wrist, and right_wrist cameras line up with, and look like, those real observations.
(2) Physical match: the simulated contact force/torque on each Sharpa fingertip, in the sensor frame, matches the logged tactile_force in timing, magnitude and direction.

What you can tune happens before simulation starts:
(1) Static object assets: realistic geometry, collision shapes, mass, inertia, friction and joints, with appearance close to the real objects, plus the initial object poses at t = 0.
(2) Offline-planned robot commands, changed only in frames where the real fingertips are near an object. Each command must stay within 0.55 rad (arm joints) and 0.65 rad (hand joints) of the logged teleop trajectory. Everywhere else, replay the logged trajectory unchanged.

No sim cheating: task objects may move only through real MuJoCo contact with the robot hands and the environment (mj_step).
Not allowed after t = 0: changing MjModel parameters; applying external forces or torques to objects; welds or equality constraints; feedforward torques beyond joint-space PD; setting or rolling back object qpos/qvel; disabling or excluding collisions; reporting contact forces that don't come from the MuJoCo solver (for example, copying the logged tactile readings).

Immediately present the reconstructed scene and rollout results as an interactive HTML session viewer with one page per episode, showing:
- At the bottom: A synced timeline (play, scrub, speed control) that drives every panel.
- On the left panel: An interactive 3D Blender scene showing the simulated robot and objects, showing contact points and force arrows as replay progresses.
- On the right panel: Real vs. sim camera views side by side for all 3 cameras. Real vs. sim finger force visualizations.
```

Plain text

Copied

### **2. Human view to simulation**

Given an egocentric human video of a manipulation task, Argon identifies the task-relevant objects, replaces crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed meshes for concave containers, and retargets the human hand trajectory onto a 76-DoF bimanual humanoid with 22-DoF five-fingered hands in MuJoCo contact physics.

Human View to Simulation — Egocentric Human Video to Dexterous Humanoid Twin: Left shows the input egocentric human RGB video; Right shows the synchronized 500 Hz MuJoCo + Blender Cycles multi-view simulation rollout.

_Prompt:_

```
[Attached: egocentric_human_video.mp4, candidate_sim_views.png, hand_3d_keypoints.json]

You are building a physically solvable 500 Hz MuJoCo manipulation environment (`scene.xml`) and studio Blender render that faithfully reproduces the tabletop task shown in `egocentric_human_video.mp4` on a bimanual humanoid robot with 22-DoF dexterous five-fingered hands:

1. Scene Reconstruction & Camera Calibration:
   - Identify only the manipulation-relevant objects (the grasped target object and the receiving container or landmark) and triangulate their 3D tabletop coordinates from the egocentric camera intrinsics/extrinsics.
   - Replace crude bounding boxes with compound convex-decomposed 3D meshes so concave containers (nested bowls, recessed wooden trays, open bins) support physical interior placement.

2. 500 Hz Dexterous Motion-Fitting Stress Test:
   - Retarget the 3D human wrist and finger keypoints to the humanoid's 7-DoF arm and 22-DoF hand joints, and step the trajectory in MuJoCo at 500 Hz (dt = 0.002s) with zero kinematic weld constraints.
   - Verify opposing thumb-and-finger force closure, clean object lift (> 2 cm), and stable final placement inside or beside the target landmark.
```

Title: Your Game Is A Harness - k-hole

URL Source: https://kylekukshtel.com/ai-harness-engineering-game-development-claude-code

Markdown Content:
I gave a 45 minute presentation entitled“Your Game Is A Harness” as part of [Indie Rodeo in Calgary](https://indierodeo.com/) on 9/12/26. After speaking with a lot of people after my talk, I thought it would be good to more broadly share the ideas I presented there in a form that could be enjoyed by people beyond just those who attended the conference.

Also, because I talk about AI a lot on this blog, people assume I use AI to write. This is not true! Everything below is 100% human authored, with me writing the post with basically only the slides I presented as a reference (this is not a transcription). As much as I enjoy using AI to write code and tools, I get a similar enjoyment out of writing“the old way”, especially as I have no reason to try and make any part of this process more efficient.

So with that all out of the way, I present to you my first ever blogification of a talk I gave. Enjoy!

* * *

## Introduction

[I give a small introduction to myself and my own work, that I’m omitting here, as you’re on my website]

I want to talk about using LLMs in game development. Not one-shot type demos that look cool on Twitter, but like _real_ development. Where you’re working eight hours a day, 5 days a week, etc.

And before I get into it, I think it’s useful to level set about LLMs. Or at least get into some basics so the rest of what I talk about here makes sense. I recognize that for a lot of this people this will be review, so if you just want to get into the dev-loop stuff, scroll down to the next section.

My journey into using LLMs for dev work started with a moodboarding site I made called [mood.site](https://www.mood.site/). This was pre“agentic” anything, but I wanted to test and see if ChatGPT at the time could actually code anything. The process was a lot of me just blindly copy/pasting code into ChatGPT’s web interface. The process sucked, but I was surprised at the results. [I built the site! It worked!](https://kylekukshtel.com/mood-site-moodboards-spite-driven-development) I still needed to verify a fair amount of stuff myself, but it was enough to convert me. If I didn’t have access to an LLM I wouldn’t have been able to make that site happen in near the amount of time it ended up taking me (~2-3 weeks of nights, probably like 20 hours total). I’d probably still be working on building the first version today.

Since then, mood has become something of a testbed for me moving through LLM stuff (and a mildly successful project on its own!), and has inspired me to kick up lots of other projects that use similar stacks. Additionally, LLMs have gotten better, especially with things like Claude Code and later Claude models. From my own experience, I feel like now there is very little, if anything, I think an LLM _can’t_ do when it comes to a web-based stack.

It could be easy to then say LLMs can do _everything_, as so much of software is web software. But whenever I tried to use an LLM on building a non-web game _thing_, it was this resounding takeaway:

## “LLMs are Bad At Games”

Any time I tried to use an LLM for a game-y thing, it would fall over. Maybe this is my own bias. I’ve been a game programmer for nearly 15 years, I think I know how things work. I can sniff out“bad” game code a mile away. But when it comes to Svelte web-apps, I’m decidedly less well versed and am inclined to think that whatever code the LLM produces is“good”. Maybe it’s _actually_ garbage. But there _is_ reason to believe the Svelte and web-stack stuff _is_ quality, in part due to the fact that there are LOTS of high quality web projects with their source available online. Comparatively for games, I imagine there are orders of magnitude less data to train on.

Not only this, but games have a lot of _stuff_ in them that isn’t code. Games aren’t just about putting static images and text in a layout. There are _tons_ of things in games that aren’t easily representable by code. _AND_ then on top of that there is all the same text layout stuff of web, but only as a subset of the 100 other systems a game needs to handle.

This is part of the reason why a lot of people have been making games in Three.js — they can easily represent assets as plain boxy primitives and skip a lot of the asset generation/conforming work and processing normally required for games. As a result, a lot of that stuff is slop because it lacks any real authorial voice outside of whatever the LLM median is.

However, maybe they have a point.

A key idea of the one-shot Three.JS workflow (as well as LLMs proficiency at building web apps) is that _everything_ is code. By having _stuff_ as code, it’s very easy for an LLM to be able to reason about it, make changes, etc.

However for traditional games, this is not the case. Or at least the full story. Games obviously have code, but there is a lot of other stuff that is _not_ code. This means that there are key components of games that are effectively opaque to an LLM. If your game then relies on the effective puppeting and transforming of that opaque stuff, then an LLM is going to fall over when trying to work on your game.

I think a lot of the gamedev community maybe gave LLMs a go a bit ago and ran directly into this. The“LLMs are bad/not useful/etc.” sentiment (massive caveat here, just talking about capability specifically and not potential society-ending implications) came from running headfirst into these limitations.

This is to say that, structurally, LLMs are bad at reading games. At least in their default state.

## LLM Basics

Let’s talk more about why, and what we can do about it.

Any call/prompt to any LLM service breaks down into three basic components. A system prompt, an assistant prompt, and a user prompt:

**System prompt:** Generic text shared across all users of a service. This usually describes the basics of the LLM itself, with something like“You are Opus 5, an intelligent Large Language Model created by Anthropic…”. This isn’t to say these aren’t important (they are), but more that they aren’t super-relevant to our use case. [You can see some examples of posted (and exfiltrated) system prompts for models here](https://github.com/asgeirtj/system_prompts_leaks).

**Assistant prompt:** This is kind of a sidecar prompt section meant to help guide the AI in terms of what it is responding to. You can think of it basically as the model’s basic“interaction” vector with your prompt, and represents something like the model’s“response” to the user based on some input. You usually do not have to think about this.

**User Prompt**: This is really The Thing. Most any input you put into any AI tool goes here. Any submitted chat, code, etc. gets dumped into this section. When people talk about“context”, they are largely talking about“how many tokens are stored in the user (and assistant) portion of a prompt”.

It may be easy to think that each chat is a“fresh” version of the above, but what actually happens is that, as you work with a model in a given session (the bounds of“session” vary based on what service you are using — this can be a single Claude Code session before closing it, a“chat” accessible in the side panel of a web hosted model, etc.), every prior message you sent to the model is re-submitted _every_ time you send a message. It’s kind of like playing the old playground game where, on your turn, you have to say everyone else’s thing _again_ before then adding your own thing for the next person to have to add on.

## Context and Context Pollution

As you do this over and over, you build up the“context” of the session you’re working in.

This is all well and good, but a key thing to notice here is that you only really are able to address the“latest” thing in your context (i.e., you submit a new message). Things from previous messages get submitted over and over again to the model. Hence, you want to make sure what’s in your context is“good”, otherwise you can find yourself in degenerate scenarios where your context becomes polluted due to“bad” things earlier continually informing new work.

Managing context then is a key thing in working with LLMs, and a new engineering practice called“context engineering” has emerged in light of these constraints. Context engineering asks“how can we get the _best_ information into the context, with as little pollution as possible”.

There [is a great blog post here on“ways long contexts fail”](https://www.dbreunig.com/2025/06/22/how-contexts-fail-and-how-to-fix-them.html) that goes a bit more into this, but I’ll highlight the key part here:

Context Engineering itself is a really big topic that is outside the scope of this talk/blog, but we will be using some of the tenets of it here to explore how to help LLMs do a better job working with games.

Said differently, getting LLMs to work well with games is a _context_ problem, not something that is intrinsically linked to how games or LLMs“are” (or“aren’t”!).

The complicating factor here though is, games are _weird_. Or at least: we have no real template to build a game. We have game engines, but there is effectively 0 standardized tooling for anything, in part because every game manifests its own needs differently from one another.

This is acutely unique to games (imo), but it manifests enough in other technological domains that a new concept has emerged in order to get agents to effectively“work” with whatever your work product is: Harnesses.

## Some Description of the Idea of a Harness

The general idea of a Harness is that it’s some set patterns of actions an agent is meant to take in response to some well (or loosely) defined expected input. You’re probably already using a harness like Claude Code, but these can be augmented, extended, distilled, abstracted, etc. to better support the _specific_ work you are trying to do. There’s also been a LOT of action in this space recently, with many harnesses being built for developing all sorts of things:

The key things these are all pointing to is:“how can I better understand _what_ I’m building, and guide that process as it is developed”. Harnesses can tie in things like iterating with a browser, telemetry, profiling, and even full SDLC work like making tickets, documents, etc.

However, the thing _none_ of these do well is actually talk _to_ your game. Your game is a bit of a black box, and most of what’s visible to an LLM is only the code-as-written, which as we talked about before, isn’t really enough. We know LLMs are already good at working with code, so it’s not like some harness itself solves that“games aren’t just code” issue we ran into in the first place.

What really needs to happen here is that we can take all the _stuff_ in games, and try to turn it _into_ something the LLM is able to work with. We need to crack open the black box of your game and make more of it addressable directly by an LLM.

Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. Parsimony measures how much code AI models add.

It takes the patches that benchmarks already publish and counts **coding units**: syntax elements like statements, calls, comparisons, names and literals. Lines aren't counted, so cramming code isn't rewarded, and deleted code is subtracted: net units = added − removed.
