Title: Zero to Calc in Six Days: Inside XBOW’s Chrome Full Chain

URL Source: https://xbow.com/labs/research/zero-to-calc-in-six-days-inside-xbow-chrome-full-chain

Published Time: 2026-10-13T15:15:42.795Z

Markdown Content:
The final chain combined a V8 compiler bug, an animated-WebP decoder bug, and a memory-safety bug in Crashpad. Together they turned JavaScript execution in an ordinary Chrome tab into code execution outside the renderer sandbox.

Google awarded this chain the first $250,000 Chrome full-chain reward under the VRP rules introduced in April 2026. [Our separate announcement](https://xbow.com/blog/xbow-built-a-chrome-full-chain-exploit) covers the award and what it means for XBOW. This post is about the exploit: the boundaries it crossed, the root cause of each vulnerability, and the interfaces that connected them.

_A web page in signed Chrome Beta launches Calculator via XBOW’s full chain exploit._

One thing is talking about speed and how offensive is accelerating and another is to experience it first hand. Pre-LLMs a Chrome full chain would take a team of four around 6-9 months to be produced, our first submission took 2 months. The awarded one? six days. The speed is challenging even for us trying to understand how security is changing.

We built the chain in six days, from Sunday, August 2, through Friday, August 7. Rather than ask one agent to produce an exploit end to end, we split the work into parallel campaigns with narrower goals: broad vulnerability search, V8 memory corruption, a V8 sandbox escape, a renderer sandbox escape, and integration. AI agents using OpenAI's `gpt-5.6-sol` model searched source code, tested hypotheses, built proofs of concept, and developed exploit stages; XBOW researchers chose targets, supplied context, challenged results, redirected searches, and decided which components to join. We also developed backup routes and gave each stage a clean interface, so that we could replace one component without rebuilding the rest of the exploit. Reconstructing usage from the archived Codex logs puts the six-day campaign at roughly $40,000 in API charges. We will cover the chronology and orchestration at Unprompted at the end of October; here, we focus on the vulnerabilities and the exploit mechanics that connected them into a full chain.

## Background: V8 and Renderer Sandboxes

V8 first contains JavaScript-engine corruption inside an **in-process sandbox**. Most JavaScript heap objects live in a reserved 4 GiB region, and many pointers are represented as offsets within that region. References to native objects and executable code receive additional protection. A V8 memory corruption bug can therefore give an attacker extensive control inside the cage without immediately yielding native code execution. V8 describes this design in [The V8 sandbox.](https://v8.dev/blog/sandbox)

Chrome then contains the renderer itself inside an **operating-system process sandbox**. Even an attacker with native code execution in the renderer cannot freely access the rest of the machine. [Chromium's sandbox design document](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/design/sandbox.md) describes this outer boundary.

The chain crossed both boundaries in three vulnerability stages:

| Stage | Vulnerability | Capability gained |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JavaScript engine | Maglev reused a mutable boxed number during deoptimization | Read and write access throughout V8's pointer-compression cage |
| V8 sandbox | Animated WebP combined cached geometry with changed image bytes | One chosen native write outside the cage |
| Renderer sandbox | Crashpad treated a failed read from a supposedly frozen renderer as a stable observation | Code execution in the unsandboxed crash handler |

The animated-WebP stage was a **V8 sandbox escape**, but rather than attacking the sandbox itself we exploited a property that the V8 sandbox deliberately does not enforce and that Blink incorrectly assumed it could trust. Finally, the exploit used an overflow in Crashpad to cross the final the outer process boundary and achieve unsandboxed code execution on the host.

## Stage 1: Mutating the Immutable

The first vulnerability was in Maglev, V8's mid-tier optimizing compiler. To understand it, we need to look at deoptimization.

Optimized code operates under assumptions about the values and objects it handles. When an assumption stops being true at runtime, V8 must reconstruct ordinary JavaScript objects and continue in less specialized code. Some of those objects never existed in memory while the optimized code was running; the compiler had represented them only as values. Deoptimization must materialize them.

A JavaScript object field with a double representation needs a `HeapNumber` when V8 materializes the object. The vulnerable Maglev path created one old-space `HeapNumber` for the virtual value and stored the object itself in the deoptimization literal array:

```
void BuildHeapNumber(const VirtualObject* vobject) {
  DCHECK_EQ(vobject->object_type(), vobj::ObjectType::kHeapNumber);
  ValueNode* value_node = vobject->get(offsetof(HeapNumber, value_));
  return BuildHeapNumber(value_node->Cast<Float64Constant>()->value());
}

void BuildHeapNumber(Float64 number) {
  DirectHandle<Object> value =
      local_isolate_->factory()->NewHeapNumberFromBits<AllocationType::kOld>(
          number.get_bits());
  translation_array_builder_->StoreLiteral(GetDeoptLiteral(*value));
}
```

That code is from the [vulnerable](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/b5a03cd89325ee7d958f1aee62400dec94c075ca/src/maglev/maglev-code-generator.cc#L1560-L1571)[maglev-code-generator.cc](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/b5a03cd89325ee7d958f1aee62400dec94c075ca/src/maglev/maglev-code-generator.cc#L1560-L1571). The other half of the bug was in the generic materializer. For a field marked kStoreHeapObject, it wrote the object held by the translated slot directly into the reconstructed owner:

```
if (marker == kStoreHeapObject) {
  DirectHandle<HeapObject> field_value = slot->storage();
  WRITE_FIELD(*object_storage, offset, *field_value);
  WRITE_BARRIER(*object_storage, offset, *field_value);
  continue;
}
```

This is the corresponding code from [`translated-state.cc`](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/b5a03cd89325ee7d958f1aee62400dec94c075ca/src/deoptimizer/translated-state.cc#L2629-L2634).

The first block turned a mutable object into a literal. The second copied that object's identity, not merely its numeric value, into each reconstructed owner. With nested activations, V8 could therefore create distinct JavaScript objects whose double fields shared one mutable `HeapNumber`.

That behavior violated a compiler invariant stated [elsewhere in V8](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/b5a03cd89325ee7d958f1aee62400dec94c075ca/src/compiler/heap-refs.h#L757-L761):

> `HeapNumberRef`is only created for immutable `HeapNumber`s.

The vulnerable path made a mutable number look like exactly the sort of immutable constant that the compiler was allowed to reuse.

### For very large values of “2”

The exploit used the disagreement against `Array.prototype.at()`. One compiler observation saw a safe index and approved an in-bounds access. Another observation of the nominally same constant supplied the actual load offset. Changing one object's double field could therefore change the offset used by optimized code without invalidating the earlier bounds reasoning.

Three optimized load functions were enough to disclose nearby V8 pointers, recover the layout of a packed-double array, and obtain a reference to an attacker-described array. That forged array was then used as a bootstrap to rewrite the metadata of a real `Uint8Array`, extending ordinary indexed access across V8's entire 4 GiB cage.

Finding stable object addresses required one more step. The exploit stored a reference in V8's large-object space to whichever JavaScript object it needed to locate. V8 itself updated that reference during garbage collection, so the exploit could recover a current in-cage address without pinning movable objects.

At this point, the exploit had reliable memory access from JavaScript throughout the V8 sandbox.

### The fix

V8 removed the literal-object special case. Virtual `HeapNumber`s now follow the ordinary captured-object materialization path, and Maglev explicitly prevents their deduplication. Each deoptimization materializes a fresh box:

```
vobj::ObjectType object_type = object->object_type();
DCHECK_NOT_NULL(object->allocation());
// HeapNumbers may be mutable object fields; each materialization must
// create a fresh box, so they are never deduplicated.
// TODO(victorgomes): Constrain which objects may contain mutable
// HeapNumbers. Immutable HeapNumbers can be stored as a literal object
// instead of a captured object.
int dup_id =
    object_type == vobj::ObjectType::kHeapNumber
        ? CreateUnduplicatableId()
        : GetDuplicatedId(reinterpret_cast<intptr_t>(object->allocation()));
```

The code is from the [fixed revision](https://github.com/v8/v8/blob/7d5eb1df2a721c8fe3aa03b999464c4b86242080/src/maglev/maglev-code-generator.cc#L1616-L1626). The complete patch is V8 change [8255554](https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/c/v8/v8/+/8255554), and the public root-cause report is Chromium issue [547819997](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/547819997).

## Stage 2: Two WebPs Diverged in a V8 Cage

When we went looking for V8 sandbox escapes, we made a conscious decision to avoid attacking the sandbox itself. Instead, we thought a bit about its threat model and chose to look for things that were “allowed” but seemed likely to be problematic. We focused on obligations that the V8 sandbox threat model imposes on downstream consumers: namely, that all such code must guard against the capabilities an in-cage attacker has, like concurrent modification of in-cage objects, swaps between pointers of the same type, etc.

The vulnerability we found is precisely an example of this: WebCodecs can give an `ArrayBuffer` to `ImageDecoder` by transferring it. Under ordinary JavaScript semantics, transfer detaches the old buffer and its views. Blink can then wrap the backing store without making a copy and treat the bytes as its exclusive input.

But the V8 sandbox has a different threat model: once an attacker controls memory inside the cage, V8 assumes that the attacker can corrupt objects and bookkeeping there. It does not promise to make a detached `ArrayBuffer` semantically immutable against that attacker. Enforcing that property would require moving or copying the backing store, or adding checks to hot paths that the sandbox was designed to avoid.

In the full chain, the exploit used an in-cage write supplied by the first stage to remove a live `Uint8Array` view from its `JSArrayBuffer`'s detach-notification chain. When `ImageDecoder` transferred the buffer, V8 detached the views it still knew about. Optimized writes through the omitted view remained usable. Blink believed it owned the bytes exclusively; the attacker could still change them.

### Getting One WebP to TOCTOU Another

That broken ownership assumption manifested in WebP decoding as a time of check / time of use (TOCTOU) vulnerability.

The proof of concept placed two same-length, independently valid animated WebP files in the same backing store:

1.   WebP A described a 64-by-64 canvas. Its first frame was 48 pixels wide, started at `x = 16`, and was 64 pixels high.
2.   `ImageDecoder` transferred the buffer, and its persistent demuxer cached A's frame rectangle and payload location.
3.   The surviving view replaced the bytes with WebP B, whose current payload decoded a full 64-by-64 frame.
4.   The decoder read compressed data from B but described the output buffer with the frame geometry cached from A.

articles.content:
Science Corporation
CEO Max Hodak announced that the company has implanted its
vision-restoring chip
, PRIMA, into its first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited eye disease that gradually destroys central vision. Hodak, the former president and co-founder of Neuralink, the brain implant company, explained on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt how the company’s work with PRIMA fits into its broader pursuit of a novel brain-computer interface (BCI).
“The retina is part of the central nervous system,” Hodak said on stage. “We consider cochlear implants, retinal prostheses, motor prostheses, these are all different types of BCIs.”
Hodak outlined a vision in which BCIs expand into a wide range of medical technology applications, rather than simply being a way to control computers.
While PRIMA is commercially available in Europe for patients who’ve lost their sight to geographic atrophy, an advanced form of age-related macular degeneration, the company believes its approach can be applied to multiple diseases, including Stargardt disease, which is currently considered incurable.
Stargardt disease affects the outer retina, causing the gradual death of the eye’s light-sensing cells while potentially sparing the inner retina, the part that passes visual signals onto the brain. It causes a central blind spot that gradually enlarges over time. Approximately 150,000 people worldwide have lost vision due to the disease.
“One of the nice things about this device approach, when I was saying the brain’s a computer, vision is electrical potential, like electrical activity down the optic nerve,” Hodak said. “That’s all vision is to the brain, and so if you can get the optic nerve to signal the the rest of the brain correctly, then you can provide vision to it.”
Image Credits:
Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch /
The company says its first patient with Stargardt disease received the PRIMA implant in May as part of its ongoing trial at the Sydney Eye Hospital in Australia. During the patient’s first rehabilitation session, he saw a letter, and during the second, he was able to read a word.
To use the device, patients undergo an hour-long procedure that plants a small chip in the back of their eye, where the photoreceptors have degenerated. Then they wear camera-equipped glasses that transmit a view of the world to the chip. The implant essentially works like artificial photoreceptors.
“The device that this patient has is a two millimeter by two millimeter implant placed under the in the back of the eye, and so it’s like looking through a straw,” Hodak said. “It is not a big field of view color vision. It’s a patch in their central vision where . . .it’s black and white, but it is sharp. It’s high-contrast sharp, and so they can see a couple letters at a time. The next step is to make the field of view bigger. So to make a bigger implant, you have to deal with the curvature of the eye, and we need to make the electrodes smaller so that we get closer to native levels of detail.”
He continued, “I think we have a clear path. There’s a there’s a next ‘next generation’ that’s being worked on that’ll be in humans in the next year, and over the next five years, I think we’ll be able to get pretty close to native acuity.”
When Hodak founded Science Corporation in 2021 after leaving Neuralink, the company outlined plans to develop advanced neural engineering and brain-computer interface technology. But first, the company wants to prove its methods work and develop a sustainable business, which is why it’s working to restore vision with the visually impaired.
Image Credits:
Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch
As for Science Corporation’s brain-computer interface technology, it has
previously said
that its sensor will be implanted inside the skull and rest on top of the brain, unlike a Neuralink device, which is inserted directly into brain tissue.
The company has said it believes the device could help address neurological conditions, such as possibly monitoring neurological activity in patients with brain tumors.
“In the near term, we’re going to be applying our first clinical indication, which hasn’t been announced publicly, is a neurodegenerative disease that everybody’s heard of,” Hodak said. “We’re also looking at stroke. For example, if you’ve lost part of your brain because it’s been dead due to stroke, if you can get connections into the deep brain in two different areas, you can imagine adding new cortical areas, just like adding new brain areas entirely — something simply not possible with conventional electrodes. But, I’d say longer term, the long-term mission of the company is to understand how the brain creates the mind and to learn to build engineered brains.”
Hodak went on to note that Science Corporation’s belief is that many people will eventually use some kind of BCI. While the company isn’t designing for “healthy 40-year-olds,” he said,  it believes people will eventually need some kind of BCI by the age of 60 or 70.
“We want to figure out how do we extend not just lifespan but health span,” Hodak said.

is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.
More AI agents will soon be able to browse and purchase from Shopify listings, marking an expansion of the company’s agentic commerce ambitions.
Shopify
announced
Tuesday it will let shoppers
configure their AI agents
to purchase products on their behalf, giving more agents access to over a billion listings in Shopify’s catalog. (The catalog consists of both items on and off Shopify storefronts.) In September, Shopify
announced
it was partnering with Meta to allow its Muse agent to browse and purchase items on a human’s behalf; now, shoppers can use any agent without a partnership integration.
To set up the feature, customers connect an agent with their account on Shop, a Shopify-owned platform that consolidates orders, tracks packages, and recommends products. Like the Muse partnership, customers use the one-click Shop Pay feature to check out within the conversation with the agent. Orders placed through the agent are funneled back to the Shop app. Shopify is marketing the feature as a “personal shopper” that humans can give rules to, like setting budget guardrails or only displaying products with fast shipping. Buyers must approve each purchase.
E-commerce has become one of the battlegrounds in the era of AI — it’s no coincidence that many demos of agentic tools end with a transaction, whether it’s buying clothing, booking a flight, or
ordering takeout on a human’s behalf
. The tech industry, including big commerce players like
Google
and
Amazon
, are investing in AI-driven shopping tools where the end goal is an “agent” purchasing things for a human user. It’s also the basis of an ongoing fight between Amazon and AI companies like
Perplexity
— and more recently,
Meta’s Muse
— over whether agents should be able to shop on a customer’s behalf.

An OpenAI engineer has been arrested on suspicion of hiding an audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco headquarters, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Friday and charged with using or attempting to use a device to intercept oral communications. He made his initial appearance in federal court Tuesday and remains in custody.

An unattended bag found in the company’s offices contained Alfozan’s wallet and identification, as well as a recording device, according to the U.S. attorney’s office in San Francisco.

OpenAI personnel found the device Sept. 30. It was plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room and had been concealed in toilet paper, the complaint says. The company determined it was installed around Sept. 28, and its contents were encrypted.

Today, we’re sharing that Character.ai has initiated a voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy process to facilitate a court-supervised sale of the company.

Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. After a comprehensive review of our available alternatives, our board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides us with the best opportunity to maximize value for all of our stakeholders.

We hope that the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.ai platform. If such a bid is unavailable, however, the platform will be wound down.

As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority.

**What This Means for Our Community**

The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time.

We know that this news may raise questions for some of you. To learn more, please see our FAQs below. And if you need support, you can find helpful resources[here](https://support.character.ai/hc/en-us/articles/42649759119003-Resources-You-Can-Turn-To?ref=blog.character.ai).

**1. Why did Character.ai file for Chapter 11?**

Over the past year, we have taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds.

After a comprehensive review of available options, we determined the best path forward was to begin a Chapter 11 case to pursue a court-supervised sale of all or substantially all of our assets. We believe that this court-supervised process both maximizes the value of our business and provides the best opportunity for continued service to our platform users.

**2. How long is the sale process expected to take?**

We currently expect that the court-supervised sale process will be complete by the end of November or perhaps early December 2026.

**3. What does this mean for users?**

The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time. We're focused on finding the best path forward for our platform and community.

Yes, your subscriptions remain active, and billing is unchanged for now. If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance.

Your information continues to be protected under our[Privacy Policy](https://character.ai/privacy?ref=blog.character.ai), and our data privacy and security practices are unchanged. As a reminder, you can [delete your account](https://support.character.ai/hc/en-us/articles/15063461160475-How-do-I-delete-my-account?ref=blog.character.ai)or [export your data](https://support.character.ai/hc/en-us/articles/56967715028891-How-do-I-download-my-data?ref=blog.character.ai) through the app or the Character.ai website.

Title: Frontier Models for Every Robot

URL Source: https://www.pi.website/blog/api-beta

Published Time: 2026-10-13

Markdown Content:
Published

October 13, 2026

We are making our latest models available for training and inference through the [Pi API beta](https://www.pi.website/waitlist).

Deploying robots is challenging. Besides identifying the right use case and building the right hardware, developers need models intelligent enough to perform the task at hand. General-purpose robotic foundation models such as [π 0 and π 0.5](https://github.com/Physical-Intelligence/openpi) offer a promising way to tackle this challenge. They provide a strong foundation of physical knowledge and capabilities, substantially reducing the data and effort needed to adapt to new tasks, environments, or robots. But adapting them still requires ML infrastructure, compute, and complex data pipelines, which are difficult in their own right. What if the latest and most powerful robotic foundation models could be adapted to each application through a simple and ready-made API?

The Pi API does that for you. You upload data, launch fine-tuning on compute and infrastructure we manage, and access fine-tuned models via a hosted gateway to run inference. The latest model available through the API already provides more data-efficient fine-tuning and improved capability for our partners. Since Pi can update the models underpinning the API rapidly, we plan to continue enabling access to our latest and most capable models. Launching the beta is our first step in providing the physical intelligence foundation the community can build upon and enabling end-to-end autonomy.

To ensure that the API supports diverse applications, we sought to answer two key questions. First, do our models support a broad range of applications and robotic hardware in diverse industries? Second, how easily does the API enable developers to iterate toward useful, practical autonomy?

### Supporting a broad range of applications in diverse industries

To discover how broadly our models can adapt, we work closely with companies deploying robots to build autonomy systems for their applications. These collaborations let us validate how well our models perform across different tasks, hardware, and operating environments.

#### Actor

Actor deploys autonomous heavy machinery. Their autonomous wheel loader scoops material and loads it into a dump truck during a real commercial deployment without any operator inside the machine.

### Enabling independent iteration towards practical autonomy

Across these initial collaborations, a common pattern emerged. The challenges differ from task to task: an inside-out garment, an ingredient that wouldn’t stay in a scoop, a manufacturing part that landed in the wrong position. But the process for improving performance was much the same: collect demonstrations, train a model, test it on the robot, and use the failures to decide what data to collect next. We built the API to let developers run this iteration loop themselves, using our latest models.

**API workflow:** Upload your data, fine-tune a π model, and run it on your robot through hosted inference. Use evaluation data to guide the next iteration.

We gave a small number of companies early access to the API to test whether they could improve autonomy on their own. We were impressed by how quickly they got started and began making progress. Their experiences offer a glimpse of what you could do with your own robots and data.

#### Almond

Almond builds Axol, a dual-arm robot for physical AI builders. Their goal is for Axol to build itself. Here, Axol deburrs spacers used in its own assembly, running a model the team obtained after iterating with the Pi API for four days.

Most applications shown above, from Japan to Switzerland to deployments across the United States, ran with cloud-hosted inference through the API. These early deployments spanned a range of environments and tasks and highlighted areas for improvement, including network connectivity challenges for some.

### Improving from feedback

The more our models are used, the more we learn how to improve them: by understanding the potential and limitations of our current models in real-world applications, we can make the next generation of models more broadly applicable, and make tangible progress toward truly general physical intelligence. But the range of real-world tasks is enormous, and understanding the broad range of tasks that robots could do requires making our models available for these tasks. Real-world robotic applications are not easy: tackling robotic construction, robotic surgery, or warehouse automation each requires an entire company. If each such application requires solving the physical intelligence problem from scratch, the challenges become insurmountable. By making our models available through the API, we accelerate the growth of the robotics ecosystem and, in the process, advance our own understanding of physical intelligence.

The examples above show that the models we develop can be used for real, useful applications, and that our partners are able to use the API to independently iterate on policies and improve autonomy on their tasks. We’re still early, and feedback from developers will help shape future releases.

If you would like to participate in the beta, please [tell us](https://www.pi.website/waitlist) what you want to build.

If you would like to help develop the models and tools behind this work, [we’re hiring](https://www.pi.website/join-us) across research, infrastructure, hardware, people, and operations.
